subject: ela
description: Students analyze how a particular part of an informational text (a sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section) fits into the overall structure of the whole and how that part contributes to the development of the ideas. They identify the organizational pattern an author uses (such as chronological or sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, description, or order of importance); locate where a given part sits within that structure (an introduction, a body section, a transition, a supporting example, a conclusion); explain the job that part does for the text as a whole (such as stating the main idea, providing evidence, defining a term, raising a problem, presenting a solution, or signaling a shift); and connect a structural choice by the author to how it builds or clarifies the central ideas. Every item embeds the full passage, paragraph, or section it depends on, so the student needs nothing external. There is no math.
subSkills: Identify the organizational pattern of an informational passage (chronological or sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, description, order of importance)
Locate a part within the overall structure (introduction, body or supporting section, transition, conclusion) and explain how you know

Name the structural job a sentence, paragraph, or section does (state the main idea, introduce a topic, define a term, give an example or evidence, raise a problem, offer a solution, signal a shift, draw a conclusion)
Explain how a specific part contributes to the development of the ideas by linking it to what comes before and what it sets up next
Recognize transition and signal words that mark the structure (first, next, because, as a result, however, in contrast, for example, most important) and use them as evidence
Distinguish a part that develops or supports the central idea from a part that merely adds a detail
Evaluate why the author placed or ordered a part as they did and how moving or removing it would change the reader's understanding of the ideas

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the organizational pattern
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short section. Which text structure does the author use to organize this information, and what signals it? Answer: It is cause and effect, signaled by phrases like because and as a result that connect the event to its consequences.

problemArchetypes.name: Locate the part in the overall structure
problemArchetypes.example: Read the paragraph. Where does this paragraph fit in the structure of the whole text? Answer: It is the introduction, because it names the topic and previews the main idea that the body sections will explain.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the structural job of a part
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence in context. What does this sentence do for the section as a whole? Answer: It states the main idea that the rest of the paragraph supports with examples.

problemArchetypes.name: Connect a part to the development of the ideas
problemArchetypes.example: Read the section. How does this paragraph contribute to the development of the author's main idea? Answer: It provides a specific example of the problem introduced earlier, making the general claim concrete and convincing.

problemArchetypes.name: Analyze the role of a transition or shift
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. What is the purpose of the sentence that begins with However at the start of the second paragraph? Answer: It signals a shift from describing the benefit to presenting a drawback, moving the text from one side of the comparison to the other.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate the effect of structural placement or ordering
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. Why might the author have placed the description of the problem before the solution instead of after it? Answer: Stating the problem first gives the reader a reason to care about the solution, so the solution feels necessary rather than arbitrary.

Easy.description: A short, clearly structured stimulus (one or two paragraphs, roughly 40 to 90 words) embedded in the item, organized with an obvious pattern and explicit signal words. The task is to identify the organizational pattern, locate the part (beginning, middle, end), or name the simple job a part does. One structural concept is tested and the relationship is stated or strongly signaled, requiring little inference.
constraints: Stimulus is one or two short paragraphs of roughly 40 to 90 words included in the prompt
Tests one concept: name the structure, locate the part, or name an obvious job (state the topic, give an example)
Identify-level task with explicit signal words such as first, because, or for example
The connection to the main idea is direct and stated, requiring minimal inference

Medium.description: A moderate stimulus (a multi-paragraph section, roughly 100 to 180 words) embedded in the item, with a structure that is present but less heavily signaled. The task requires analysis: explaining how a specified part contributes to the development of the ideas by linking it to other parts of the text, or explaining the purpose of a transition or shift. The student must reason about how the part functions within the whole, not just label it.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-paragraph section of roughly 100 to 180 words in the prompt
Tests how a part develops or supports the central idea, with the relationship implied rather than stated
Analyze-level task: explain the part's contribution by relating it to what comes before or after
Distractors are plausible but confuse the part's job (for example, calling a supporting example the main idea, or a transition a conclusion)

Hard.description: A complex multi-part stimulus (a passage with two or more contrasting sections or a complete short informational text, roughly 190 to 280 words) embedded in the item. The task requires evaluation: judging why the author structured the text as they did, comparing the function of two parts, or explaining how a structural choice (the chosen pattern, the ordering, a placement, a shift) shapes the development of the ideas. Requires inference about authorial intent and the effect on the reader's understanding.
constraints: Stimulus is a passage with contrasting sections or a complete short informational text of roughly 190 to 280 words in the prompt
Tests the effect of a structural choice (pattern, ordering, placement, shift) or compares the roles of two parts
Evaluate-level task: justify why the structure works or how a change would alter the reader's understanding of the ideas
Requires inference about authorial intent; distractors reflect partial or surface readings of the structure

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student summarizes what the part says instead of explaining what the part does for the overall structure
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answers by restating the information in the excerpt rather than identifying its structural job, such as introducing the topic, supporting the main idea, or signaling a shift

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misidentifies the organizational pattern, choosing one that does not match the signal words or the relationship among ideas
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a passage that lists causes and consequences as compare and contrast, or calls a step-by-step sequence a problem and solution, ignoring the actual signal words and logic

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a supporting detail or example with the main idea, or treats the main idea as just another detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies a specific example sentence as the section's main idea, or claims the topic sentence is merely one detail among equals

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misjudges where the part falls in the structure, confusing an introduction, a body section, a transition, and a conclusion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls an opening paragraph that previews the topic a conclusion, or treats a transition sentence as the introduction of a brand new topic

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats each paragraph or section as a standalone unit and fails to relate the part to the whole text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Explains the part only on its own terms, never linking it to the main idea or to what came before or what it sets up next

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student overlooks transition and signal words and so misreads the function of a shift
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Ignores a word like however or in contrast and treats a contrasting paragraph as if it simply continues the previous point instead of marking a shift

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes the part's placement and the text's order are arbitrary and cannot explain the author's structural choice
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the order does not matter or that the part could appear anywhere, ignoring how placing a problem before a solution or building from least to most important shapes the reader's understanding
